source.title: Interpreting Video Representations with Spatio-Temporal Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies sparse-autoencoder features in video vision representations. It does not test whether individual neuron poles have one main job, the share of such poles, or the quality of neuron explanations on unseen activations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports measurements of SAE-feature monosemanticity and temporal coherence in video; these are related to interpretability but are not measurements of individual neurons or neuron poles. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. Other reported results, such as action-probe accuracy, ablation effects, and text-video retrieval, do not measure the claim’s named constructs.
record.test_reason: The study trains sparse autoencoders on DINOv2 and VideoMAE video features. It scores SAE-feature monosemanticity, temporal coherence, probes and retrieval. It never examines individual neurons or neuron poles, never audits job shares, and never scores neuron explanations on held-out activations. It does not cite or rely on either original source. No version of the claim is tested or used, so T6 applies. The relation is set to cites_only only because no enum value means 'neither cites nor uses'.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that standard SAEs give monosemantic video features but destroy temporal coherence. Contrastive weight gives a controllable trade-off between reconstruction and coherence, and no variant dominates. Own-space MS contains a backbone-alignment artifact. Hard TopK selection remains the open problem.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains sparse autoencoders on video-backbone activations and evaluates SAE-feature metrics; it does not use the neuron-pole audit or held-out neuron-explanation testing described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: MonoSemanticity Score values differ between each backbone's own feature space and the independent CLIP similarity space. Temporal coherence varies across SAE variants and configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Own-space MonoSemanticity Score for SAE features is about 0.97 for VideoMAE versus about 0.32–0.37 for DINOv2. Under a CLIP similarity space, every variant scores about 0.67–0.68. The authors call this a backbone-alignment artifact.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Monosemanticity scores for SAE features depend on the similarity space used, so cross-backbone comparisons with own-space MS are unreliable.

fits_no_version.finding: On DINOv2/SSv2, standard TopK SAE encoding lowers lag-1 autocorrelation from 0.435 to 0.277. Contrastive and Matryoshka variants recover some of this, and one Temporal+M configuration reaches 0.462.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hard TopK SAEs make video feature activations temporally incoherent, and temporal contrastive training can restore coherence.

record.peer_reviewed: The paper gives the venue as Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM ’26).
record.problems: The reported monosemanticity results concern SAE features, not individual neurons. The paper notes that the own-space metric is not directly comparable across backbones and that the CLIP similarity space is not claimed to be objectively neutral. Main analyses use two backbones and SSv2; the authors report 3 seeds and note that maximum standard deviations were 0.3 pp for probe accuracy and 0.005 for R².
record.rows_left_out: Other results, including action-probe ablations, retrieval results, and additional reconstruction and classification metrics, were left out because they do not measure neuron-pole job shares or held-out neuron-explanation performance.

untested.parts: All of it: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares (about 90% one job, 7% two, 2–4% unexplained).
All of it: neuron-pole shares across language models, dense versus MoE, and scale.
All of it: the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
All of it: neuron interpretability shares as a function of architecture, regularization and tools. The vision work here concerns SAE features, not neurons.
All of it: neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
All of it: whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on held-out data.
All of it: simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: This is an SAE-feature study on vision and video backbones, not a neuron study. It does not mention the 'Neural Networks Are Already Clean' essay or the OpenAI neuron-explanation work. Table 2 MS for the standard SAE (0.359) differs slightly from Table 1 (0.365), probably from a different configuration or run; this is irrelevant to the claim. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares and the proportion of poles with one or two jobs or not yet understood.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, model scale, and neuron-pole shares.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Neuron interpretability shares, the proposed causes of messy neurons, and the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict where neurons fire on held-out activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by predicting activations on new text.
